pages.text: Mungi, a young water buffalo from the lower village, lifted Dingding's bamboo basket. "That's mine!" Dingding reached out both hands. It was full of young rice plants Dingding wanted to carry.
Dingding shoved Mungi with both hands. "I was going to carry it!" Mungi staggered, and the basket fell onto the bank with a thump.
Young rice plants spilled across the bank. Mungi pressed their mouth shut and went away. Dingding's hands were left empty.
Mom, who worked several paddies on her own, sat on the bank and gathered the plants. "When you pushed, the basket fell and Mungi left. Don't Push—Use Words!"
"Lower your hands like this, and open your mouth this wide." Mom opened her mouth wide. Dingding lowered both hands and opened their mouth. "Like this?"
Dingding went to Mungi, hands down and mouth open. "I wanted to carry the rice plants, too. I'm sorry about earlier." Mungi's mouth formed a circle. "...I wanted to carry them, too."
"Then let's carry them together!" Mungi offered one side of the basket. Each held a side, and they walked slowly along the bank. Don't Push—Use Words! Not a rice plant shook.
The basket felt much lighter than when carried alone. Dingding sniffed and looked up at Mungi. "Talking is so much easier than pushing!"
When Mungi reached for the water jug first, Dingding lowered both hands. "One, hands down! Two, open my mouth wide! Three, say what I want!" "Mungi, I'd like a sip, too."
Mom hugged Dingding with one arm and Mungi with the other. Pushing left you alone; talking brought a friend to carry things with. "Don't Push—Use Words!" Dingding called boldly.
